utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Madam Registrar, good morning to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen, I can follow the proceedings in my mother tongue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Good morning to you. Appearances -- what happened to Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Wubben is in the building and will be joining us after the first break. I am Patricia Sellers on behalf of the Prosecution, and with me is co-counsel, Ms. Joanne Richardson, and our acting case manager, Sanja Bokulic. And good morning to Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is he looking for Rule 68 material, Ms. Sellers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am not allowed to divulge that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Vasvija Vidovic. Together with Mr. John Jones I appear on behalf of Mr. Naser Oric. With us are our legal assistant, Ms. Adisa Mehic, and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you Madam Vidovic, and good morning to you and your team. Welcome back, Mr. Jones. Before we bring in the witness, we were discussing yesterday, Judge Brydensholt, Judge Eser, and myself, about when the Defence case is going to come to an end. Two recent phenomena is -- one is that each time we get a new witness almost always the estimated time for the evidence increases, if it doesn't double. It's true that there is now a motion to drop some witnesses and to add two, with the estimate that ultimately it will save us about seven days of testimony. I take it that as regards the number or the witnesses that will be dropped or that the Defence is seeking to drop, I don't think I need to have any reaction from you because that's not exactly your business under our Rules. However, I would like to know if you oppose for the production of the two witnesses, one of whom definitely it would be extremely strange on your part if you did because he is the calligraphic expert. And the other one I would like to know whether you are -- as regards the other witness whether you are opposing the production of that witness or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as regards to the witness who was the subject of a proper filing of the 92 bis motion, I believe we informed the Trial Chamber yesterday we would oppose. As to the proposed forensic expert, we will of course have to wait to see his report, to see his qualifications, and I imagine upon the filing of a proper 94 bis motion we'll be able to evaluate that. My understanding that will be at least 30 days before proposed testimony. If we have no problem with his report and qualifications, it might be a similar situation that we had with Dr. Stankovic, that we will just have the report allowed to come in as evidence. If there will be some controversy, we will make sure that we address that with as little delay as possible. In regard to the other 92 bis witnesses that were proposed within the Defence counsel motion to add and to drop, we have not been able to see any statements regarding what they would testify about via 92 bis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, it's -- let me butt in. Forget the 92 bis because the 92 bis I think Mr. Wubben has already informed the Trial Chamber that the Prosecution would be opposing --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Only one at this point in time. The other two we haven't been able to analyse --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But this is not 92 bis. This is an ad hoc motion, separate motion, that was filed by the Defence to drop six witnesses and to bring forward Professor Bilic, and that -- I've heard you. I've heard your comments. And Ejub Golic, who was present at a prisoner exchange which has been referred to in evidence during the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: -- that would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That would be?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: A viva voce witness one who would come to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And we certainly don't oppose the Defence adding that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So let's deal with this straight away, that as far as the two witnesses, Professor Bilic and Mr. Ejub Golic are concerned, you're authorised to produce these witnesses. With regard to Professor Bilic, I don't think we need more information as to what the subject matter of his testimony will be. As regards Mr. Ejub Golic, I think we need a summary of what -- of the facts that he will be testifying upon and the expected duration of his testimony. The other thing is this: Assuming for argument's sake only for the time being that some of the witnesses that you have asked to produce pursuant to Rule 92 bis will need to be brought over, in other words that the motion will be turned down, rejected. We basically are going to lose the benefit of those seven days that you mentioned in your motion. So we would be -- notwithstanding the dropping of six witnesses, we would be back to square one. Our concern, therefore, is that we need to make sure more or less towards the end of this week or early next week that we have a target date, revised target date, because we did have one but because of different circumstances obviously that has to be shifted a little. So we need to know exactly from you when you expect to finish your case, and please try to be as practical and cooperative as you can. In other words -- and don't misunderstand me. I'm not saying that you are doing this. But if you sincerely think that a witness needs three hours to finish his testimony, don't tell me that you need six or five or seven. All right. So try to stick to what is barely necessary because then we'll have a short meeting. If necessary, I will even ask my SLO to have a 65 ter meeting with you if I see that there are problems. And we will need to have establish a final day -- date within which your case has to come to an end. Also, although this is, I admit, a little bit premature, if you think that following the resting of the Defence case you intend to bring further witnesses in rebuttal, if you have that in mind already, please let us know. Of course there will always be reservation that we are still a couple of months away from the resting of the Defence case and anything could happen then and need for a rebuttal may arise during the course of these next two months or so. So what I am asking of you and of Mr. Wubben is that if you are in a position already to tell us: Yes, do expect a rebuttal, then we will need to prepare for it. This is what we are asking of you. Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will inform you as soon as possible. We are taking such issues under consideration now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. I would imagine so. Yes, I would imagine so. So that is why I have asked. But if you already have one, two witnesses in mind, it's good for us to know because we can plan ahead with more sense. All right. Any further preliminaries? Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I will be brief. I omitted mentioning yesterday when we discussed the length of testimonies and why on occasion the time doubles, the reason is as follows. We carefully studied the list and you know that before the last motion when we gave up six witnesses, prior to that we had given up three other witnesses. In any case, we continue doing this and we will do it in any case when we realise that we have covered a certain territory with a given witness and that we do not have to call another. It is in case of this witness, he was supposed to testify for three hours and he was to cover what other two witnesses were supposed to say. But still, I believe his testimony will be shorter than the three would have been cumulatively. And we will strive to do the same thing in the future. It is in the best interest of our client to act in this way, and we want to see the end of this trial as soon as possible. Apart from that, I had another preliminary issue, and I wanted it to be recorded in the transcript. Yesterday evening and this morning we received the list of potential exhibits to be used by the OTP. I wanted to use this opportunity to mention this before we bring in the witness. We object as to the authenticity of the following documents proposed by the Prosecutor and they intended to use them with this witness. For -- we object for all the reasons we mentioned previously. All of them come from suspicious sources of the government of the RS, and we mentioned that on several occasions and we will come back to it in more detail at a later stage via a motion. I wanted to specify the documents. This is first and foremost 03729742 to 03729742 entitled "statement of Jovanovic, Rajko." Then exhibit 03721259 to 03721259 entitled "list of soldiers for commendation from the Potocari Brigade." This document has not been brought in through any given witness. Its source is unknown and it doesn't have the date or the address, and one cannot understand who put the document together. Then document 03720834 and 0372208 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters missed the last figure.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the report of the military police, the document being from the collection of the intelligence service of the RS. It hasn't been introduced through any witness, and it is not to be found on the list of the documents tendered and hasn't been presented through Witness Radojcic. One cannot be certain as to the author. There is no stamp and no trace of author. Then the list of TO Gostinj members, document number being 02116725 to 02116728. We managed to establish that pertaining to an entire spectrum of documents on the EDS that the source was the government of the RS, and there was some extracts, certain pages, which belonged to the overall collection of documents. The date is 1995. There are several lists in several periods of time, and it is unclear exactly what the period was pertaining to this document. And one cannot see who the author was. It's a piece of paper that could have been written by anyone at any time. Then document 02116772 to 02116773. Then list 7510/1 Stari Grad, that is the title. There is no date, there is no signature on the document. We don't know who the author is. And in our view it could have been created at any given point in time. It is a document coming from the government of the RS. Then 03720963 to 03720965, "the warpath of the Potocari Brigade." We were able to see that the OTP has received this recently from the government of the RS. There is a list of documents received previously from that government, and that document doesn't appear there. From the list, one cannot see to whom the documentation was addressed, we cannot see the source, and we cannot establish the author and the time of its production. It hasn't been presented through any testimony. There is no heading, no stamp, no signature, and it does not belong to a -- any collection that we could use to establish its source on the EDS. That is why we object as to the authenticity of this document. Then document 02116776 to 02116777, "killed soldiers of Stari Grad TO." That part of the documentation begins with the heading "source, the government of the RS," hence we object to the authenticity and the entire collection comes from 1995, but one can see that there are temporal overlaps in the collection and it is unclear what the exact date of production is. There is no heading, no stamp, no signature, and no date. For us, it is but a plain piece of paper. Then diary of an unknown author, number 04231845 to 04231872. We don't know the author. We don't know the time when the alleged diary was created. And in the document different time intervals appear. A part of it pertains to 1992 and then it skips to 1995 and then goes back to 1994 and then to 1993. It contains descriptions completely unrelated to the area or the time period. There is not a single piece of reliable data as to the author or as to the time of its creation. That's why we object to its authenticity. And then the last document, I believe. It is 035929085 [as interpreted] to 03593050, "proposal for commendation to the soldiers of the 8th Operations Group." It fell under the daily disclosure category by the OTP, and the document has not been introduced through any of the OTP witnesses or through any of its investigators. We don't know the source, and hence we object as to the authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic. All this has been recorded. I may have made the mistake, but I don't think I have. I think you skipped the fifth document on the list, the one with the ERN 02116774. You told us nothing about that. I am -- I'm saying this subject to correction. If you did and I missed it myself, my apologies, but I don't think you did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is quite likely, Your Honour. It is document 02116774 to 02116774, "unit Stari Grad." It has no heading, no date, no signature. It is unclear as to the time of production and who the author was. That's why we object to its authenticity as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if we might briefly explain the Prosecution's position. Firstly, we'd like to remind the Trial Chamber of your own decision in regard to the admission of evidence and believe that both parties will be bound to the manner in which documents are admitted and then later weighed. So I will not go into those arguments. In terms of some of the specific objections of Defence counsel, might the Prosecution first put forward that because a document is unsigned doesn't necessarily mean that a document is not valid. We produce documents every day, whether in this courtroom, whether in notes, that we do not sign. Many records that are normal business records are not signed. In addition, documents that do not have dates on them do not necessarily mean that the document in itself is not valid or is a document that is not credible. I would remind the Defence that they have submitted documents in yesterday's proceeding, Defence Exhibit 916, Defence Exhibit 912, and there we have a variance in whether the document is signed, whether the document has a date, whether the document has evidence of who and where it was produced. I would also like to state quite frankly that it seems that we have the double standard of when documents come from the government of the Republika Srpska that assist the Defence, whether it be documents related to armed forces, whether it be documents related to lists of their soldiers who have been wounded or killed, they seem to be quite valid. They seem to be placed before a witness and asked for a Defence exhibit number and admitted and not questioned in regard to the source. If the Prosecution then submits a document that might be similar in the type of content or similar in terms of where it came from, the Republika Srpska or the government, that seems to be a per se in validity of the document. And this Prosecution sincerely and seriously objects to any standard the Defence might be putting forward in that regard. We would also like to say, and this is in general terms, that the admission of documents in this proceeding via investigators has been one manner in which documents have been entered into the record, and the other manner, such as we did see yesterday during the Defence examination of the witness, is to show witness a new exhibit, have the witness look and comment upon it, and ask that that document be admitted. Prosecution would certainly like to have the same standard applied in terms of admission. If the Prosecution were to be required to produce the investigator each time it had a new document or decided to use a document as the evidence develops, I believe that would be an unfair burden on the Prosecution. I would certainly say it's an unfair burden on the Defence in order to make them put all their documents in through investigators. The practice of this Trial Chamber has certainly been one that adds to the ease of admission, allowing Your Honours then to judge the weight. If I might then talk about some of the specific documents. I'll go to the one that Madam Vidovic mentioned that is a statement coming from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Sellers, sorry to interrupt you. Usher, could you please go to the room where the witness is waiting and explain to him that we are discussing a procedural matter that is not related, as such, to his testimony, and extend our apologies to him and put his mind at rest that he will soon it called. Thank you. Yes. Sorry, Madam Sellers, for interrupting you like this, but I have a suspicion that this is going to be -- to prolong a few more minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No more than a if you more minutes, Your Honour. One of the documents that the Defence was questioning and I have part of the ERN number 03729742. I'll have to refer back to the record. That relates to a statement taken by -- as Your Honours will find out, someone who is a Bosnian Serb. I strenuously object to it, but yet if one would go to D135 I believe is the number the Defence has admitted themselves a statement taken by a Bosnian Serb, by Bosnian Serb authorities, and that has been used to show that Defence evidence might have some credibility, weight or validity. The Prosecution will be doing that same sort of exercise with this document. And then we have the other document, 03721259, a list of soldiers for commendation. Your Honour, this seems to be a document that you will see that's produced in the normal course of army business, noting which soldiers have been valid, which soldiers deserve merit. We also have a document that's relating to members of a TO unit. Now, the Defence's complaint seems to be the source, seems to be the timing of the document. It will certainly be explained through evidence if the document is a compilation of information that dates in between 1992 and 1995. First, that doesn't affect the validity of the document. One might keep a document and a running record on a document of the changes that have happened with the TO or with the company between 1992 and 1995. So I think that the Defence objection there is not only completely valid, I think the fact that there is information from that entire period actually assists the Trial Chamber in looking at the evolution of evidence and in particular will assist the Prosecution in putting forth its evidence that's relevant and pertinent to this case. The Defence hen makes objections concerning a document entitled the warpath. Now, we can certainly ask and see whether the warpath is something militaries produce to show which troops have been in which battles and which battles have been participated in. I do believe that that very phrase has come up within the Defence case, and to say that it has no stamp on it, has no significance, Your Honour, I would once again revert to my prior arguments. We do have a document that is entitled "soldiers from Stari Grad." I believe it can be put before Your Honours and Your Honours can determine whether that list of soldiers is relevant. We say it is relevant because the names on the list have come up before and it corroborates and confirms evidence that we have put forward. Then we have a document -- and I can understand the Defence's concern about this document because of the information it contains. That document is a diary of an unknown author. If I might put forward just one small correction. It is not made by one author, as Your Honours will see, it is information taken down by several data-entry clerks, in particular a man named Huso Oric, whose name we will find in other documents, who seems to have assisted other record-keepers and other names of military men that tell what was, in essence, the history of certain brigades and TOs. It is normal and natural that that document does not have one author because several companies have been asked to put down their war history. It is a document that Your Honours will see discusses attacks that are relevant to this indictment, discusses persons that have come up frequently within this trial, and also discusses a temporal evolution of many of the TOs and the companies. The Prosecution would submit that its relevance certainly could not be questioned by its mere source of coming from the Republika Srpska or by its form. I will state one thing the Defence did not say in that the document is original is in handwriting. The Defence has submitted even yesterday a partial document that was in handwriting and translated, so certainly that doesn't make a document invalid. As a matter of fact, it might lead to its credibility to show that it had several authors and many of the authors do note they were data takers. Your Honour, then the last document that you mentioned in relation to Stari Grad, I would go back to my previous arguments that it contains information that's relevant. You will see that the Prosecution will be putting forward a bit of a wider look at a particular company, group of soldiers, combatants, fighters, TOs, in particular from Stari Grad, and we believe that witness might be able to assist us with some information on those documents. For those reasons, Your Honour, I ask that we stick to the normal procedure that this Trial Chamber has recognised within your decision and within the practice that both parties up until this time period have been allowed to proceed upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I will give the floor to the Defence, but before I do so, so I make it clear, to be honest with you both, I wasn't expecting this intervention from the Prosecution because basically my understanding is what should be your understanding as well, namely that we have committed ourselves with you that the admissibility issue proper of each and every document that is standard will be made at the end of these proceedings when the case of the Defence is rested, when we've heard final submissions, pleadings, and then I told you - I don't know if you were present here last time - that the question of admissibility, final decision on admissibility, will be our first deliberation. That's number one. The rule being in this Tribunal that unless on the face of it a document is manifestly inadmissible and should not be admissible, then we admit it with the caveat that I mentioned earlier, that the probative value to be given to it will come at a later stage. The second understanding is that preferably if, say, Madam Vidovic stands up and tries to introduce a document in -- to -- in the records and puts it in front of the witness and, if possible, we avoid any submissions, any arguments on the admissibility issues relating to that document in the presence of the witness. So the suggestion that I have made in agreement with my two colleagues and which has been adopted so far is that if there are new documents to be tendered, that we are made aware of -- we haven't seen these documents ourselves. Obviously you both know the contents of these documents, but we don't. And if the Defence has been put on notice that you intend to tender these documents in the course of your cross-examination today of this witness, then if they have objections relating either to the authenticity or, in any case, relating to the admissibility of these documents, they should make that clear or make their submissions before the witness enters the courtroom. So then we will have it on record, we will know -- and you would know that these documents are being challenged, and we can proceed with the witness as if nothing has happened, as if these documents are not subject to any challenge at all. Of course, with the understanding that the Defence can ask any questions that they like on the authenticity, or on the relevance, maybe, of these documents. And the same applies to you. Now you have been put on notice before the witness comes in that these witnesses [sic] that you intend to use are being challenged. So if you have any questions to put to the witness in relation to the admissibility issues that have been raised, you're free to put them. But otherwise, please, let's leave the final submissions on categories or particular exhibits -- categories of or particular exhibits till the stage -- till the appropriate stage, which will come much later than now. All right? Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was going to reply just briefly because I also wanted to mention a preliminary matter on another issue, on 92 bis, but very briefly. Certainly that helps our understanding because my understanding certainly was that we were to make timely objections to authenticity and that we weren't to remain silent until the very end of the trial because when you're talking about thousands of exhibits, if then in March or April we then mention all our objections, Your Honours will not have had the benefit of knowing those objections when the witness was here. So I'm not sure whether Mrs. Sellers is saying that this is not timely to make these points or that they're not relevant. Certainly in terms of relevance, whether a document is signed or whether there's a stamp, those are relevant factors to waive admissibility, and I'm not sure if the Prosecution's submission is that under all circumstances these are utterly relevant. Obviously they are relevant, and we're obviously going to note those as we go along. And since Ms. Sellers did deal substantively with these points, I would just, basically in a line or two, deal with each of the points she made. In terms of documents from Republika Srpska, there's no double standard. There's a distinction which should be very clear and easy to understand, which is documents produced by the Republika Srpska, their own documents versus documents which they allege that they've seized from the Bosnian sources. That's obviously a very clear distinction. As far as their own documents are concerned, firstly, there simply is that distinction; but secondly it's a fact that as with confessions and declarations against interest, documents which are not in the interests of the maker to make them are often deemed more reliable because there's no incentive for an army to tell lies about its own activities necessarily. Whereas here we say there is an incentive for the Republika Srpska to claim to have seized documents from the Bosnians, precisely for this case. And just so Your Honours understand the fear we have is that there may be, for all we know, and I'm not saying that this is the case, but a unit in Republika Srpska which is busy following our case and dashing off documents and sending them off and in that way helping to build a case against our client. We say that is not an absurd suggestion. It is a distinct possibility, and that is something which this Tribunal has to guard against. And certainly if you have a document which you have no idea who produced it, when they produced, how they produced it, then how can Your Honours be sure that someone isn't just dashing off documents and sending them to this court to be used against our client. As far as the question of the use of an investigator is concerned, it is important that there is an investigator because they talk about the source so we actually know where the document came from. Obviously there are two issues. A witness can attest to the truth of the contents of a document and therefore give that document weight. But if there is no investigator, so no information about the source, it's shown to a witness and the witness says, Well, this simply is not true, then in our submission the document at that point has absolutely no value because you have no idea where it comes from and it hasn't been confirmed by a witness. And that's why we point out when an investigator hasn't produced a document, not that it's a requirement but it's relevant for those purposes. As far as statements taken by the Serb authorities of Serbs, D135, we of course used to impeach that witness. And again, I hope that's a clear distinction that our exhibits, they're not all exhibits we stand behind as truthful. We've introduced exhibits for a whole variety of purposes which will be clear from the context. If we introduce prior inconsistent statements, obviously it's for that purpose, for showing -- for impeaching that witness, not necessarily for the truth of the contents of that document. So that has to be taken into consideration. And finally - possibly finally - Ms. Sellers has in fact been giving evidence about some of these documents. She says that one of the exhibits today was produced in the course of business. Of course in a national jurisdiction you need a witness to come along and say this was compiled in the course of business. It's not enough for counsel just to say this was produced in the course of business or these were data entry clerks. Well, how on earth do we know whether they were data entry clerks and not some forger who put this together? Again, it's -- this Tribunal certainly has a certain flexibility with exhibits, but it's not to be -- the proceedings are not to be brought into disrepute by just allowing any old -- any old approach to be taken to documents, and I submit that we should actually have regard to national practice in terms of actually witnesses being brought to give evidence about whether this was indeed put together in the course of business, whether indeed these were data record clerks, and indeed why -- if that weren't the case, why did the Prosecution bring witnesses like the investigator and Radojcic and others. They themselves sought to show that their documents are reliable, and in that spirit Your Honours will of course have to assess whether they've done that or not. And finally, as for the sort of general submission that, well, the Defence did this and so we're doing the same, well, if the Prosecution has submissions about the weight or admissibility of our documents, they're of course free to make them. There's obviously no tit for tat, that if there's some document which they think is not very credible for X reason, they have a right to introduce an equally incredible document. That submission holds no water in my submission. As I say, I wanted also to mention this, Your Honour, wishes me to address you further on that point. Just on 92 bis, and I think it's important to make this point, we actually -- in the interests of saving time, we have quite a few 92 bis applications in mind in the pipe-line, but we are in fact, to be honest, waiting to see how the current one is pending, and that's for this reason: That we're concerned about the test which is going to be applied or being applied to the phrase "other than the acts and the conduct of the accused" in 92 bis. You will have seen in paragraph 7 of our motion we say that the concept would be stretched way too far if any aspect of life in Srebrenica was considered to be outside the provisions of Rule 92 bis. But we're waiting to see Your Honours' ruling on that, and we may, to be perfectly -- to be perfectly honest, we may appeal if -- if we consider that we're going to be blocked in introducing a dozen or so 92 bis statements by an overly restrictive approach. And I also say that because Your Honour had mentioned that at this stage of the trial we should all have in mind which areas have been more or less established. Mr. Paris deals with a lot of issues which we thought, certainly the Trial Chamber and perhaps the Prosecution, would consider had already been established about life in Srebrenica. A great deal of evidence has been given on those matters, and so we do wish to wait and see what Your Honours' ruling is and then decide whether to proceed with our other applications, because Your Honours' ruling will indicate to us the prospects of success for our other applications. And we don't want to submit half a dozen applications if we can tell that they are going to fail. So that's just to indicate that we are holding back with those applications until we know what the test is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Regarding 92 bis, you all know because you heard Mr. Wubben say so yesterday and day before I think that we are to expect the Prosecution response shortly. So when that comes more or less we would know what's the basis of the opposition of the Prosecution for the production of that one witness under Rule 92 bis. With regard to the matter of admissibility, I don't think it's the case, Judge Brydensholt, Judge Eser, of saying anything further. Basically these are pleasures yet to come, and we'll deal with this matter as we go along, particularly towards the end. But please do remember, in case you have forgotten it, that more or less not more than a week ago I expressed my concern about this matter and explained to you that at some point in time we would appreciate having from both of you an itemised and detailed explanation of the documents that you are objecting to -- I mean, they are all on record already, but to make sure that we have them all, we will require a list of all the documents that you are objecting to. And I remember Mr. Jones saying that you had precisely this in mind and that you would be coming up with such a document -- you had in mind of coming up with such a document --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Towards the end of trial, I thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course towards the end of the trial. There is no point in trying to articulate all this before when the number of documents is increasing by the dozen every day. I think we can close this matter here now. I think we are all fine-tuned on the practice of this Tribunal as regards admissibility of documents, and our intention is to continue following this practice. With regards to the other points that you mentioned and mentioned, I think -- I don't think we need to discuss them here, about signatures, stamps, et cetera. If you read the decision in Brdjanin, over which I presided, the judgement in Brdjanin, more or less I dedicated a whole chapter in that judgement on -- to the basics of admissibility, and there you would read enough what was the position of the Trial Chamber in that trial as regards authenticity issues such like signatures or absence of signatures, absence of stamps, absence of dates, handwritten documents, absence of supporting evidence. Anyway, I don't think we need to go any further into this. We can adjourn on this matter, and we can bring in the witness unless there are other matters that you would like to raise. I see none. So, usher, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So take your time, Ms. Vidovic. And do you think you will finish your cross-examination today? I don't think so now, at this point

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can guarantee I will not finish it today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I like such guarantees, especially involving Fridays, as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you will finish tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I will try earnestly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir. Welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I apologies to you on behalf of the Chamber for keeping you waiting for practically an hour before you could come in and continue with your evidence, but we had serious business to transact here on procedural matters that do not involve you, so you don't need to worry, but we needed to discuss a few issues before we could continue with any other business in this trial. So welcome once more. Ms. Vidovic will continue with her examination-in-chief, and when she finishes, which should be in roughly about two hours' time, then Ms. Sellers will start with her cross-examination. We will have to continue tomorrow, and it is expected that we will take the entire sitting tomorrow. Hopefully if you try to keep your answers brief and if we don't have any major calamities we should finish with your testimony tomorrow and you would be free to go home tomorrow. So let's start, Ms. Vidovic, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Vidovic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday we talked about the document dated 5 January 1992 containing an order to cleanse Konjevic Polje, and we left it off there. I wish to correct myself, though, it was dated 5 January 1993. First of all, I'd like you to clarify a detail that was not entered into the record correctly. On the first day of your testimony, we talked about a decision issued by the Serb forces you stated were located in the area of Banjevici. It was entered into the transcript as having happened in -- at the end of 1992. And now my question to you is whether this happened at the end of 1991 or at the end of 1992, namely the training of Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The training of Serb soldiers took place at the end of 1991, not at the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I merely wanted to correct the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can have the usher's assistance now, please, in showing the witness a document by the Drina Corps command dated 7 January 1993, sent by the command of the Drina Corps to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, signed by Commander Milenko Zivanovic bearing the ERN 04267256.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I will read out the first part of the document, namely item 1: "Enemy." "During the night the enemy engaged in minor provocations by directing mortar fire at units of the Zvornik Brigade." Now, please look at the relevant portion of the document which is as follows. "In the morning the enemy conducted a powerful attack on the units of the Bratunac Brigade in the Kravica sector from the axis of Kamenica-Maricici, Sandici-Kravica, and Bukovo Glava-Jezestica, and by 1200 hours had succeeded in taking control of the village sectors of Marici, Siljkovici-Kajici, and Jezestica." First of all, do you know anything about the events transpiring on the 7 January 1993 relating to Kravica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 7th of January, 1993, in regard to Kravica, I know that there were attacks on Glogova and Bljecava and that we received some information from Ejub Golic - I was told so by Sabic - that they had been attacked up there. I don't know how they learned about this, perhaps from the civilians who were up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So you are somewhat familiar with these events. I want to ask you the following. Based on your knowledge and in fact what is -- it is stated in the document, namely: "In the morning hours the enemy conducted a powerful attack on the units of the Bratunac Brigade in the Kravica sector from the axes," and so on. My question to you is as follows: Do you know whether on the 7th of January, 1993 it was the civilians in the Kravica area and their facilities that were attacked or the units of the Bratunac Brigade, as stated in the document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Kravica is concerned, civilians were never attacked there. There were no civilians there. It was the Bratunac Brigade units that were under attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall whether you went into the Kravica area at some point during the day? You started saying something about this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 7th of January Vezir Sabic asked whether anyone could assist in the area of Konjevic Polje to fire back at the artillery, which was most destructive, in order to reduce the intensity of the attacks against Glogova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a group of persons who headed in the direction of Kravica with Vezir Sabic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some 100 people volunteered to set out towards Obackici because that was where a ZIS pack, Howitzer was located, in order to possibly destroy the ZIS and reduce the intensity of the attack against Glogovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you join the group that set out for Kravica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I joined the group to assist those people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what time of day it was that you set out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the early morning hours that we set out for Obackici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what point you managed to reach.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we came closer to Obackici, there was artillery at Siljkovici, in the direction of Siljkovici, that noticed us and turned its weaponry toward us and started opening fire with full intensity, also from Obackici. On the occasion Vezir Sabic and some ten other men were wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do thereupon? Did you personally go back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A group stayed behind to maintain the position, whilst most of us returned as there were many wounded. We returned to the Brekinja [phoen] hill above Sandici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Vezir Sabic seriously wounded on the occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was seriously wounded and we had to take him back towards Konjevic Polje. However, I omitted to say that while we were on that hill an enormous mass of people emerged. There must have been more than a thousand people, all civilians, including women, who were heading towards Kravica and we tried to explain to them that there was no way for them to reach Kravica, or rather, Obackici, although we could not dissuade them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This large group of people you described, were they Muslim civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they observe the wounded that were among you, including Vezir Sabic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one man who was closest to us and he could see how many wounded we carried. However, there was no way of stopping them. They continued towards Kravica, that's to say Obackici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you specifically tell them to head back, not to continue on their way because of the attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was several lads who went over to try to persuade them not to proceed. However, they were almost stampeded over as the crowd went on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened with those civilians, this crowd of civilians, in Obackici thereafter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Having taken Vezir Sabic to Konjevic Polje, I returned towards Kravica. As I was coming closer to Obackici, I saw a large group of dead civilians. In the village of Obackici we found many civilians who were collecting food and some were leading cattle towards Sandici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were talking about Vejz Sabic not about Vezir Sabic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Vejz.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, regardless of the casualties and large numbers of dead civilians, they nevertheless managed to cross the fire line and enter Obackici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you've understood me well. There was this location called Jezero above Obackici. The civilians entered Obackici without paying attention to their left flank, whether there was anyone. As we followed in their suit, we heard fire from the direction of Jezero, which meant that there was still some Serb forces up there but the civilians simply paid no attention to this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did I understand you well? Regardless of the fact that they were getting killed in the process, they still continued searching for food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'd like the witness to be shown a new document which is an extract from a book called "Bloody Christmas" by Boro Miljanovic published in the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I will quote a small portion from page 110.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Vidovic, because we haven't yet given a number to the previous document that you used.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll admit this first. And this document consists of four pages, two in B/C/S, two in English, with ERN 04267256 to 257, both numbers included, both pages included. This is being entered as and given Defence Exhibit Number D937. Yes, before we -- you proceed with your next question, Madam, Judge Eser has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Since there are -- the witness told us about movements between Konjevic Polje and Kravica and then you also talked about Obackici, could he perhaps indicate say -- or tell us the distance between Kravica and Konjevic Polje and how he got back and forth between these two places. And also, could he perhaps locate on the map this village or hamlet, Obackici, the distance from Kravica and on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's take them one by one. Witness, can you tell us the distance between Kravica and Konjevic Polje, please. We are not interested in the distance as the crow flies but the real distance if one has to travel from one place to the other.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the centre of Konjevic Polje to Kravica, the distance is some six kilometres by asphalt road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So next is if you could locate on the map the village or the hamlet of Obackici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obackici are not on the map. However, I can explain the exact location in relation to Sandici.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot show you the exact location because it is not entered into the map, but I can tell -- I can show you the approximate location of Obackici. This is Sandici, and in this direction here lies Obackici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you perhaps mark it with an X?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. For the record, the witness marks with an X the location, which according to him, represents Obackici and that is 2.00, 2.00, from Sandici. Thank you. And the last question that Judge Eser has asked you is to explain how, on the occasion that you mentioned, you went to and from Kravica and Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: My question was not only with regard how you normally would come back and forth, but on the occasion which you mentioned on what way you came from Kravica to Konjevic Polje and back. You mentioned a certain event when you took somebody from Kravica to Konjevic Polje, then you went back again. By what means you did it? Did you walk? Or did you go on this horse-cart, as you told us? Or how was it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. In the meantime, registrar, please, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you, Witness, please if you could answer now Judge Eser's question which is directed specifically to the occasion that he mentioned to you or that you testified about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I answered the first question previously and now I will answer the latter question. It was in the suburbs of Kravica near the village of Sandici that Vejz Sabic was wounded and we took him to a place called Brekinja above Sandici. And then after having met the civilians that I talked to you about, I, together with others, took him to Urkovici. In Urkovici we had a horse-drawn cart, again, that we were able to transport Sabic and others further on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Your next question, Madam Vidovic. And the document -- the exhibit that you would be using has already been circulated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I will quote a small portion from page 110, second paragraph, which says: "On the tragic day when the Kravica defence was broken and Kravica fell, its commander incidentally was sub-lieutenant Lazar Ostojic." Here is what he says about it. But I will not read this, I will rather read out a relevant part on page 112, starting from third paragraph, which says: "By 2.30 p.m. our intervention squad was in Siljkovici. In the event of the arrival of fresh forces, they would have enabled them to join the battle. When they were about to be surrounded by the Muslims, I ordered them to move to another position in order to try to stop the evil-doers who were advancing from the direction of Glogova. In order to prevent the Muslims from advancing towards the village centre, I went, along with five soldiers, to the house of an inhabitant, Vaso, and from there we fired at them. Then I went back to the communications centre to see if the promised help was to arrive. The communications officer had already destroyed the equipment. The storage with defective weapons had already been mined and the equipment that could not be taken was destroyed within Osa. The enemy was already entering the centre of the village. In the battle we were withdrawing at the last moment, saving the newly brought wounded. Some of them died later on a stretcher or in an ox-driven cart. The last group of soldiers, including myself, left Kravica at about 4.00 p.m.. The last defence line to retreat was the one at Jezero, which was abandoned at 4.15 p.m. when it was already getting dark and when all hopes were buried. "Following the column of the army and people, I felt like the deadest of all corpses at the back of a dead column. This should also be known. On that day, 22 crates of ammunition were distributed from the storage, over 400 shells, more than 5.000 rounds for an anti-aircraft gun." In connection with this you told us that you were very much familiar with the Kravica area. Can you tell us whether you know the area where the house of this resident, Vaso, who is mentioned here is located?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But could we first move into private session, Your Honour, for a while before the witness answers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's move into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe the location of the house.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As one passes through Obackici, there's a valley there and then a hill upon which lies Vaso's house. And a bit downhill from that house there is Rahman Muminovic's estate and house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time you were moving through the centre of Kravica, did you have any experience connected with the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As we went past Obackici - and I told you what happened with the civilians there, we saw them collecting food and leading cattle - I saw that there was no Serb military presence there and I headed towards Vaso's house. In the immediate vicinity a barrage fire from automatic weapons and machine-guns could be heard. Abid Olovic [phoen] from Konjevic Polje was close by and he got killed there. At that point, I went over to a dirt road where we lingered on waiting to see what was going to happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you pause there, Witness. Did the shooting come from this particular house, as described in this book?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from that house precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you relate to us any other experience you had in terms of shots coming from houses or something related to that locality.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that neither the civilians nor we paid much attention to Jezero, which is a feature above Sandici, where the Serb forces were still present. Having heard these shots, we also heard shots up at Jezero.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, were they opening fire from Jezero upon you or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were firing upon us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, did you manage to reach the centre of Kravica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We proceeded toward Kravica. We tried to circumvent this particular house because we knew that there was army inside. We went across a wooded area and reached Kravica. We found throngs of civilians there collecting food in the houses there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you manage to come closer to the school -- the two school buildings you mentioned earlier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in retrospect I would have acted differently, but as I was going towards Kravica I -- my only thought was to get hold of a rifle because I knew how important it was to ensure my own safety. I had handed over my weapon earlier on, but as we reached Kravica we found quite a lot of weapons there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you manage to learn anything about any communications equipment? Did you find any such equipment there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We found some communications equipment; however, it was completely destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before I move on to a different document, could this document be assigned a number, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly, Ms. Vidovic. This document which consists of four pages in Serbo-Croat, consisting of a photocopy of the cover of the book mentioned earlier in the evidence, the title page, and then photocopies of pages 110, 111, 112, and 113, together with the corresponding translation into English of the title page -- title pages and cover and an extract from page 122 -- 112 is being tendered, marked as Defence Exhibit D938.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could the witness be shown two documents at once, D470 and D471. Both documents are dated 9 January 1993, and both originate from the command of the Bratunac Brigade and both were addressed to the Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, please first look at D470. The number is 04272539. It says: "To the Drina Corps command, chief of communications, chief for intelligence. Subject: Report on communications equipment lost in Kravica. "We hereby wish to inform you that on 7 January 1993 the following communications equipment in the village of Kravica fell into enemy hands." And then listed therein are -- is radio equipment, telephone equipment, charging equipment, and it is stated that the report was compiled on the basis of a statement by the signals operator of the 3rd Kravica Battalion Milo Milosevic." According to this statement, part of the equipment was destroyed by bursts of fire from two automatic rifles. Does this correspond to what you learned as you reached the Kravica communications centre there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please look at the other document which says: "Report on the disappearance of communications documents." It says: "On 7 January 1993 in the village of Kravica, the following communications documents fell into enemy hands: "Work plans," and so on, they're all listed here. At the end it says: "The code names of the corps and the Bratunac Brigade have been deciphered, broken into." In brackets it says "Idila and Gigant." "Report compiled on the basis of a statement by the signals operator of the Kravica Battalion." Based on what you observed and experienced there and learnt there, did you hear of any communications documents having been lost -- or rather, having been found there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that some such documents were found, but I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you hear that such documents were found from others who were there with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said they were found.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps this would be a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Ms. Vidovic. We'll have a 30-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It never rains but worse. Welcome, Mr. Wubben. And I'm welcoming you -- first to welcome you and secondly also for the record. There have been some changes. The plenary is no longer going to be on the 6th but it is going to be on the 5th. That would clash with our afternoon sitting of the 5th. I have had meetings in the meantime. If it is at possible, we would try to sit half an hour in the courtroom where the Appeals Chamber will be sitting on the day in the Nikolic case half an hour after they finish, which could allow us the possibility to sit up and until 3.00 or 3.30, obviously with breaks. I'm not quite sure that that is possible, but I'm working on it, and I would appreciate your cooperation on that, otherwise we will have to skip the 5th and start with that witness on the 6th. The other thing is, assuming that we would finish with this witness tomorrow, if you could start with the next witness on Monday instead of Tuesday, and we'll try to make an effort and finish with that witness on the 29th rather than on the 20th -- on the 30th, which would allow me the possibility to travel where I need to go on the 30th, as I'm having a lot of problems finding a flight and making adjustments. Thanks for your cooperation, and we'll talk about this at some later point in time, either today or tomorrow. Yes, Witness, let's proceed. Sorry to bother you with these problems. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just wanted a correction to be entered into the transcript. It was at 11.39.49 I asked the following question of the witness: Is it correct that the witnesses surrounding Siljkovici -- that the villages surrounding Siljkovici, that these Muslim villages were attacked from Siljkovici itself? And the transcript reflects whether Siljkovici were the target, which is absurd. The witness mentioned that the surrounding Muslim villages were under attack from Siljkovici and that Kravica was attacked from Siljkovici. I just wanted to offer this clarification. And this is yesterday's transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you understand me when I asked you this question -- when I asked you whether the Muslim villages were attacked from Siljkovici and not the other way around?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those Muslim villages were attacked, but I wanted to mention one thing that I feel obliged to say and I forgot to mention it yesterday, if I may offer an addition. When Ibrahim Muminovic and Salih Mustafic were killed, on that occasion my house came under direct fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. First, the date when this happened, and whether we need to redact. I don't know. Do you wish to see a redaction? I don't think it is quite necessary because there is no indication of place, but anyone who knows where these people were killed, I don't know. It doesn't necessarily --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It doesn't necessarily mean that his residence is where they were killed. I mean, so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. What was the date when this happened, when these two persons were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those two persons were killed I believe in December, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And your house was destroyed or was hit on the same day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to explain -- I just wanted to say that it wasn't destroyed but rather that it was targeted in the events that transpired. On that occasion, a Howitzer shell entered through the window and it didn't hit anything inside the building directly, but rather it ricocheted off a closet and then exploded in the middle of the room.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, and hence remained unexploded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that was great luck for my wife and children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You didn't answer the question whether that occurred on the same day those two persons were killed or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, on that same day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you. Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, just before the break we stopped at the point when you said you entered Kravica and that you were looking for weapons, and you said you found some. Where did you find it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The weapons were usually to be found in various houses. There were machine-guns and rifles, and I took a rifle for myself because I didn't want to remain without a rifle any longer because it was becoming increasingly difficult. There was some spent cartridges in the houses which would mean that they were using the houses primarily to open fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you mean -- when you say "casings," do you mean spent cartridges?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time when you were in Kravica, were there lots of Muslim civilians in it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Kravica there were vast numbers of Muslim civilians. I can't be specific as to the number, but it must have been over 1.000 and they were searching the houses looking for food. And they took away the cattle they found.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was their behaviour like, if you can put it briefly for the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I happened to be close to some people who said that they found lots of food in one house and they stampeded into their house and they paid no attention what was happening to the person next to them. They were running to get to the food, to get some for themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that day in Kravica itself, were there wounded or killed Muslim civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to Kravica, the shelling was still ongoing and there were lots of killed and wounded civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was shelling Kravica at that time, Muslims or Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbs were shelling Kravica from Banjevici, Ocenovici, Popovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you remain for long in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed until night -- the night, and when it got dark I retreated with the other people back to my village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you retreat with other armed men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, most of those who were armed returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They retreated or they withdrew?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time you spent there, and as far as you could see, did you see any house on fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't houses on fire in Kravica that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you something pertaining to the civilians. You said that that day the civilians were there looking for food. In the next few days, were you able to observe whether civilians from your area, or in general, whether they went back there, whether they came to Kravica, took some stuff away, or whether they were doing anything there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They kept bringing out food and cattle, and there were people who even -- even took off tiles from the roofs of the houses because there was lots of damaged houses in Konjevic Polje and the surrounding villages. So a lot of things were taken out of Kravica to repair the houses previously damaged in Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "lots of stuff," do you mean construction material and similar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fighting in the area of Kravica, did it conclude in December 1992? When I say "the area of Kravica," I mean the entire territory of the local commune with its villages.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fighting did not cease around Kravica. In Kravica itself, it did stop, but around it there was still fighting in Popovici, Colakovici, Jezestica. I pray your forgiveness if I keep mentioning Siljkovici, but that sticks in my mind the best. Banjevici, Colakovici, Popovici, that's where the shelling was coming from and that's where the fighting resumed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show another document to the witness by the Drina Corps command dated 11 January 1993. The title is "interim report to the Main Staff of the Army of the RS." While we're waiting for it to be distributed, I wanted to quote the relevant portion. "Interim report. "According to the report that has arrived from the Bratunac Brigade command, it is not clear who is controlling the villages of Popovici and Colakovici. I will find out and inform you. We understood that we controlled four villages. "The 3rd Battalion (Kravica) has again abandoned his position and some of the men have arrived in Bratunac. The men are angry and armed, and there is a danger of disorder breaking out in the town itself." Witness, please pay attention to the date. It says 11 January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we for a short while move into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's move into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And this document, which consists of two pages, the original in B/C/S and the other one in English, being a translation of it, is being marked as Defence Exhibit D939. ERN number is 04267279.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, related to this I wanted to ask you something else concerning Popovici and Colakovici. If one were to claim that Popovici and Colakovici were set on fire by the Muslims on the 8th of January, 1993, would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would not be correct in any case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to show another document to the witness dated 11 January 1993. It is a Bratunac command document sent to the Drina Corps command. To gain some time while we are waiting for it to be distributed, if you could kindly observe carefully, I wanted to read the following: "1, the enemy. "During the day carried out operations with groups of 15 to 20 soldiers on the Colakovici-Popovici-Banjevici-Mandici-Gornji Polom-Caus- Pobrdje-Potocari-Zuti Most axes. Their probable intentions are to use the forces from Glogova to break out into the Drina valley in the Polom sector." Witness, this portion I read out, does it confirm the situation on the ground on the 11th of January or, rather, that it was then that Muslims were active in the area of Popovici and Colakovici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am unclear about the question. Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Is it correct that the fighting around Popovici and Colakovici occurred as late as the 11th of January, as specified by the document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we assign an exhibit number to this document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document which also consists of two pages, the original in B/C/S and the other one being an English translation thereof, with ERN 04363068 is being tendered and marked as Defence Exhibit D940.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to play a video excerpt now. This is P317. We made a transcript of our own pertaining only to the relevant portions of the conversation in the excerpt. And one can clearly see what the date of the recording is. We didn't have the time to do the full transcript, and we are interested in the images themselves rather than the conversation. But in any case, if necessary, we can submit a full transcript at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I would kindly ask you to follow the recording, but wait first for the transcript to be distributed, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We may start. Your Honours, this portion of P317 begins at 35.31, and we will stop at 35.40 for the transcript. Please play the video.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "We are recording on the 11th of January or the 12th of January, 1993."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you hear the person say that they were recording on the 11th or the 12th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please continue with the video. Your Honours, for the transcript, we will continue with 41.07 to 41.30 -- no, 41.07 to 41.37.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "He is 55-years-old. We shall give him some information. Just say 55 years. We are a volunteer."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot decipher the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We -- when we viewed the excerpt, it was far better. I don't know what happened with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, were you able to see the excerpt and I believe you also saw it during the proofing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Vidovic, because if this is not to your satisfaction, perhaps we may address it to the technicians and we will have a playback. I don't know if there is a reason why we have such bad quality transmission.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, Your Honours. But I can see with the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you recognise this area on the video?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I'm very familiar with the terrain and with the area, I'd say this is a part of Banjevici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Banjevici a hamlet of Kravica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the part you said -- or rather, is Banjevici the village you said that the Serbs used to open fire at you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we continue with the excerpt, please, to see if it gets any better. We are very interested in what follows. The time is 41.54 to 42.47.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "That means this is Banjevici, or Banjevici, whatever you prefer."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, did you hear the man say "this is Banjevici or Banjevici"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Next to the village itself, in the upper part of Banjevici, this is where they fired this mortar off. It is 60-millimetre. And what we could see is the village of Banjevici, being the target.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we continue with the video.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Release the safety off -- no, not there."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were quite familiar with the area of Banjevici. For the Chamber, please could you tell -- could you say what this piece is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an anti-aircraft machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The anti-aircraft machine-gun and the mortar you saw, how far were they from the houses that we can see in the recording? Since you know the area well, are there any more houses nearby?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There are houses on the other side, too, to the left of this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Vidovic, for the record, because you did not mention the part of this last excerpt from the video, the last portion that we've seen is -- starts at 42.47 and finished at 43.39.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we give this transcript a number?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And this transcript, which is one page in B/C/S and one page in English, will become Defence Exhibit D941.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in your testimony I showed you on several occasions some documents mentioning the fact that the artillery was firing from the area of Banjevici at Hrncici and as well as your village. I will not mention the name of it. Concerning the positions we saw in the recording, as far as you know, were they used to fire at you in November and December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D005 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely at that time and throughout the year I'd say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the location at Banjevici?
